title: The Awkward Middle Between Mastery and Becoming
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli addresses the disorientation leaders feel after a promotion, when hands-on mastery gives way to ambiguity, relationships and supervision. Her central claim is that this discomfort is not a defect to be fixed but the sign of a new learning curve that demands a different identity and a different way of seeing. She reframes seniority through the Zen idea of beginner's mind, arguing that leaders should keep asking real questions and make their learning visible. She then offers three shifts (self-compassion over self-critique, psychological flexibility over self-improvement, deliberate practice over grind) and three practices for the transition: narrate the change, borrow other people's eyes, and schedule compassion. The piece ends with a one-dollar paid worksheet, but the essay itself stands as a coherent argument about identity and learning at the next level.
points: Promotion trades immediate mastery for wider perspective, so the felt loss of competence is a predictable identity stretch rather than evidence of failure.
Beginner's mind (shoshin) is presented as a posture leaders keep, guarding against the overconfidence and narrowing that expertise brings.
The author argues that senior-level bottlenecks are clarity, not effort, so working harder should give way to deliberate practice of sub-skills such as stakeholder mapping and decision memos.
Psychological safety and humble inquiry are the two conditions she names for a scope jump: model fallibility and ask questions you genuinely cannot answer.
Concrete practices: narrate the role change to your team, recruit three people who see differently to poke holes, and schedule post-meeting self-compassion.
quotes: Each step up trades immediate mastery for wider perspective. That trade is real and it hurts because identity is sticky. When the work changes, your story about who you are has to stretch or it will snap.

In organisations, this looks like leaders who ask naïve questions on purpose, who show their working, who treat hypotheses as provisional. It also looks like the humility to say “I don’t know yet — let’s run a small experiment.
We devour productivity hacks, add apps, set 4:30 a.m. alarms. That might even be helpful, sometimes. But what we really need is to stop treating discomfort as evidence of defect.

Promotions bring new tasks, but, more than that, they introduce new meanings. Adult development research suggests we grow by moving what used to have us (our assumptions, reactions and roles) into what we can hold and examine.

Narrate the change. Say your own version of this to your team: “Here’s what’s changing in my role; here’s what I’ll need from you; here’s where I might drop the ball while I learn.” That honesty earns you time to grow.

When the ground under you feels unstable, don’t rush to fix it. Take it as a sign that you’ve reached a new level of complexity; one that asks for slower thinking, clearer questions and more trust in the people around you.
